steps.body: A **multiple** is a landing spot when you skip-count. Count by 4s — 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 — and every number you land on is a multiple of 4. Multiples march on forever; there's no biggest one. Factors are few and finite; multiples are many and endless.

widget.prompt: Tap every number that is a multiple of 5 (a skip-count-by-5 landing spot).

hotspots.feedback: Skip-counting by 5 goes 20, 25 — it skips right over 22. 22 ÷ 5 leaves a remainder, so it's not a multiple of 5.
The 5s land on 30 then 35 — 33 falls between. 33 ÷ 5 has a remainder, so it isn't a multiple.

widget.missFeedback: Multiples of 5 are the skip-count landings: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25… all end in 5 or 0.
widget.successFeedback: 5, 15, and 40 are all skip-count-by-5 landings; 22 and 33 fall between the steps.

predict.prompt: Skip-counting by 5 — which digits can a landing spot END in?
predict.reveal: Fives land 5, 10, 15, 20… — the ones digit flips between 5 and 0 forever. That last digit is the whole test.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents multiples.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for multiples must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines multiples.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: 51 ÷ 3 = 17 with no remainder, so 51 IS a multiple of 3 — skip-counting by 3 lands on it.
The no-remainder test settles it: 3 × 17 = 51, so 51 is a multiple of 3.

options.label: Yes — 51 ÷ 3 = 17 with no remainder
options.feedback: 3 × 17 = 51 exactly, so skip-counting by 3 lands on 51 — it's a multiple.

options.label: No — 51 is an odd number
options.feedback: Odd numbers can absolutely be multiples of 3 (like 9, 15, 21). The test is the remainder: 51 ÷ 3 = 17, none left over.

options.label: No — 51 doesn't end in 3, 6, or 9
options.feedback: The last digit doesn't decide multiples of 3 (12 and 15 are multiples). Check the division: 51 ÷ 3 = 17 exactly.

options.label: Only if you round it
options.feedback: There's nothing to round — 51 ÷ 3 is already exact at 17. That clean division makes 51 a true multiple.

steps.body: Factors and multiples are the **same fact seen from two ends.** In 6 × 4 = 24: 6 and 4 are *factors* of 24 (they build it); 24 is a *multiple* of 6 and 4 (it lands on them). It is about direction, not size: if A divides evenly into B, A is a factor of B and B is a multiple of A. Every number divides itself evenly, so it is always its own factor and multiple.

explanationVariants: 8 divides evenly into 32, so 8 is a FACTOR of 32; 32 is what 8 divides into, so it's the MULTIPLE.
Builders are factors, the built number is the multiple: 8 builds 32, so 32 is the multiple of 8.

options.label: 8 is a factor of 32, and 32 is a multiple of 8
options.feedback: 8 divides evenly into 32, so 8 is the factor; 32 is what 8 divides into, so it's the multiple.

options.label: 32 is a factor of 8
options.feedback: That's backwards — a factor divides evenly into its number and never exceeds it. 8 divides evenly into 32, so 8 is the factor and 32 is the multiple.

options.label: 8 is a multiple of 32
options.feedback: A multiple is what a number divides evenly into, not what divides into it. 8 divides into 32, so 32 is the multiple; 8 is the factor.

options.label: They're both factors of each other
options.feedback: The relationship has a direction: 8 divides evenly into 32, so 8 is the factor and 32 is the multiple — not the other way around.

widget.prompt: Sort each number by its relationship to 6.

items.feedback: 2 divides 6 evenly (6 ÷ 2 = 3), so 2 builds 6 — a factor.
Skip-counting by 6 lands on 18 (6, 12, 18) — a multiple.
6 × 5 = 30, a skip-count landing — a multiple of 6.

widget.missFeedback: Numbers that DIVIDE evenly into 6 are its factors; numbers 6 divides evenly into (skip-count landings) are its multiples.
widget.successFeedback: 2 and 3 divide evenly into 6 (factors); 6 divides evenly into 18 and 30 (multiples). Direction decides it, not size.

explanationVariants: 12 is on both skip-counts: 3, 6, 9, 12 and 4, 8, 12 — the first spot they share.
The smallest number both 3 and 4 land on is 12 (their least common multiple).

widget.prompt: What is the SMALLEST number that is a multiple of BOTH 3 and 4?

commonErrors.feedback: 7 added 3 + 4 — but a shared multiple is a skip-count LANDING both hit. The first shared landing is 12.
24 is a shared multiple (both land there), but not the SMALLEST — 12 comes first on both trails.

widget.fallbackFeedback: List multiples of each (3,6,9,12… and 4,8,12…) and find the first they share.

hints: Each light blinks on its own multiples: red on 4s, blue on 6s.
They flash together on numbers that are multiples of BOTH.
Find the smallest shared multiple of 4 and 6.
explanationVariants: Red flashes at 4, 8, 12…; blue at 6, 12, 18…; the first second they share is 12 — the smallest common multiple of 4 and 6.
Both skip-counts first meet at 12, so the lights flash together after 12 seconds.

widget.prompt: A red light flashes every 4 seconds and a blue light every 6 seconds. They just flashed together. After how many seconds will they NEXT flash together?

commonErrors.feedback: 10 added 4 + 6 — but they meet on a shared MULTIPLE, not a sum. The first common landing of 4 and 6 is 12.
24 is a time they'd both flash, but not the NEXT one — 12 comes first on both light's trails.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Smallest number both 4 and 6 land on: list 4,8,12… and 6,12…

takeaways: A multiple is a skip-count landing — no remainder when you divide.
A factor divides evenly into a number; a multiple is what the number divides evenly into — same fact, two directions.
A common multiple is a spot two skip-counts share; the smallest is the LCM.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Multiples are the **footprints of skip-counting.** Count by 7 and every footprint — 7, 14, 21, 28 — is a multiple of 7. To test any number, divide: no remainder means it's a footprint (a multiple); a remainder means you landed between steps.

explanationVariants: 20 ÷ 4 = 5, no remainder, so 20 is a multiple of 4.

options.label: No
options.feedback: Skip-counting by 4 lands right on 20 (20 ÷ 4 = 5 exactly) — so it IS a multiple.

options.label: Only with a remainder of 2
options.feedback: 20 ÷ 4 = 5 with NO remainder. That clean landing makes 20 a multiple of 4.
